title: Telecom and Connectivity Solutions
subject: NETWORKING
description: Leased lines, broadband, internet links, IP telephony and EPABX, service level metrics, and how to structure telecom contracts.

lessons.title: Connectivity options for business
lessons.body:
Business connectivity options include:

- **Broadband:** shared access at lower cost, with variable speed. Suits small offices and non-critical use.
- **Leased line:** a dedicated link with committed bandwidth, symmetric speeds, and a service level. Suits head offices, data centres, and critical branches.
- **Fibre and wireless links:** physical or radio links for specific site needs.

The choice depends on how much bandwidth is needed, whether speed must be guaranteed, and the cost of downtime.

lessons.title: Service level metrics
lessons.body:
Telecom contracts are judged by measurable service levels:

- **Uptime:** the percentage of time the service is available, for example 99.9 percent.
- **Mean time to repair (MTTR):** the average time to restore service after a fault.
- **Latency and packet loss:** important for voice and video.
- **Committed bandwidth:** the speed guaranteed, as opposed to best effort.

An uptime figure must be read with its measurement period. A percentage over a month allows more downtime than the same percentage over a day, so compare like with like.

lessons.title: IP telephony and EPABX
lessons.body:
An EPABX (private branch exchange) is an on-site telephone system. IP telephony carries voice over the data network, using the same switches and internet link as other traffic.

When moving voice to IP, plan for:

- Enough bandwidth per call, with quality of service (QoS) set to prioritise voice.
- Power backup for phones and network equipment, so calls still work during an outage.
- Number porting and emergency calling requirements, which must be confirmed with the service provider.
- Handsets, extensions, and call routing for each site.

lessons.title: Structuring telecom contracts and discovery
lessons.body:
Telecom contracts run for fixed terms, usually one to three years. Check the start date, early termination charges, price escalation clauses, service credits for missed service levels, and the process for raising faults.

Discovery questions:

- Which sites need connectivity, and what bandwidth does each use at peak?
- What does downtime cost per hour at each site?
- What is the current contract term, cost, and renewal date?
- Is voice on a traditional EPABX, and is it planned to move to IP?
- Which service levels must the contract guarantee?
